parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 1. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a man asking a friend for advice about places to visit with his family. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 4. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 4. Tom: Hi Kate, have you got a minute? My parents are coming to stay next weekend with my sister's little boy, and I've got no idea where to take them. You've lived here much longer than me, so I thought you might have some ideas. Kate: Oh, lovely. How old is your nephew? Tom: He's seven. And my parents are in their sixties, so nothing too energetic. Kate: Well, the obvious place is Westbrook Farm Park. We've taken our kids there loads of times. Tom: I think I've driven past it. Is it on Carter Road? Kate: That's right, just before you get to the bridge, right next to the river. Tom: And what's so good about it? Kate: Well, it's got the usual things, sheep, goats and a few chickens, which are fine, but what makes it special is the horses. If your nephew's keen on horses, it's the best place around. They've got about twenty of them, and the children are allowed to help brush them and feed them. Tom: He'd love that. He's always drawing pictures of horses. Kate: Then that's perfect. It does get quite busy at weekends, though, so try to get there early. Tom: Is there somewhere to eat? Kate: There's a café, but to be honest it's overpriced and the food's nothing special. I'd take your own food. There's a lake in the middle of the park with tables all around it, and it's a really nice spot for a picnic. Tom: Great, I'll suggest that. Have you got any other ideas? Just in case the weather's bad? Kate: Well, if it rains, you could try the Glasshouse. Tom: The Glasshouse? What's that? Kate: It's a huge conservatory in the town centre, in Market Street, opposite the library. It used to be part of the old botanical gardens. Tom: Oh yes, I know the building you mean. What's in there? Kate: It's full of tropical plants, palms, banana trees, orchids. When you walk in, it's warm and humid, and it really feels as if you're in a rainforest. They used to have a section with desert plants as well, but that closed a couple of years ago. Tom: My mum would love that. She's a keen gardener. Kate: And the guides are brilliant. They really know their stuff, and they're good with children too. You do have to book tickets online in advance, though. They don't sell them at the door. Tom: OK. Is it easy to get to? Kate: The only real problem is parking. There's hardly any nearby, so I'd get the bus from here. It stops right outside. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 5 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 5 to 10. Kate: Oh, and there's one more place I should mention, the Brackley Centre. Tom: I haven't heard of that. How do you spell it? Kate: B, R, A, C, K, L, E, Y. It's a centre for birds of prey. Owls, hawks, falcons, that kind of thing. Tom: Where is it? Kate: It's out of town, about twenty minutes' drive. You go past the reservoir, and it's right on the edge of a forest. It's a lovely setting. Tom: Sounds it. Kate: It's run by Sam Holloway. You know, the man who used to present that wildlife programme on TV. Tom: Oh, really? My dad used to watch that every week. Kate: Well, he might even meet him. He's often around. And the nice thing is that all the birds there have been rescued. They were either injured or abandoned, and most of them couldn't survive in the wild. Tom: That's good to know. Do they do flying displays? Kate: Twice a day. And they only use native species in the displays. You won't see any eagles or vultures from abroad. Sam's quite strict about that. Tom: Is it expensive? Kate: It depends when you go. A full-day ticket is fifteen pounds, but if you go after one o'clock, it's twelve pounds each, and you still see the afternoon display. Tom: So twelve pounds for the afternoon. That's not bad. What about food? Kate: There's a small café. I haven't eaten there myself, but I've heard it's fairly basic. Sandwiches and crisps, that sort of thing. Tom: Well, that's fine. Thanks, Kate, that's really helpful. I think my parents will like all three. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a beekeeper called Joanna Reid talking to a group of people at the start of a beekeeping course. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Joanna: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Hillside Apiary. My name's Joanna Reid, and I've been keeping bees here for about fifteen years. This morning I'm going to give you a bit of background, then we'll go into the equipment room, and after lunch, if the weather stays fine, we'll open up one of the hives together. Joanna: People have been collecting honey for an extraordinarily long time. There are rock paintings in Spain, thousands of years old, that show someone climbing up to a wild bees' nest to take honey. But what I find really interesting is that keeping bees isn't like keeping other animals. You don't need fields or a barn. In fact, some of the most productive hives I know are on the roofs of office blocks in the city. A few square metres is really all you need. And of course, you can't tame bees or train them. They simply carry on doing what bees have always done. Joanna: So why do people take up beekeeping? When I ask people on these courses, many of them say they'd like their own honey, of course. But recently, more and more people tell me they're worried about what's happening to bees in general. You'll have read about bee numbers falling because of pesticides and disease, and people feel that by keeping a hive, they're doing something to protect them. I think that's a lovely reason, although I always point out that wild bees need help too, and planting the right flowers in your garden is just as useful. Joanna: For me personally, the best thing about beekeeping is the way it makes me pay attention to the natural world. I notice when the lime trees are flowering, or when there's been a dry spell, because the bees tell me. It's completely changed the way I see the countryside. The honey's nice, but it isn't why I do it, and it's certainly not a way to make money. Joanna: Now, most of you have never been near a hive before, and some of you might be a bit nervous about being stung. That's completely normal. Bees are generally calm if you move slowly and gently, and in all my years, I've only been stung a handful of times, usually when I was in a hurry. Actually, the people who have the most trouble aren't the nervous ones at all. It's the confident ones who rush and make sudden movements. Joanna: One practical point before we go on. Please don't wear any perfume or aftershave this afternoon. Bees find strong smells confusing, and it can make them defensive. We'll give you a protective suit, gloves and a veil, so you don't need to bring anything special, but do wear long trousers and closed shoes. Joanna: And finally, by the end of the course, some of you will want to get your own bees straight away. We can't sell you any bees ourselves, I'm afraid, but everyone who completes the course can join the local beekeepers' association for a year at half the usual price, and they'll put you in touch with an experienced mentor. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Joanna: Right, so this is our equipment room. The first thing you'll notice are the hives. Most beekeepers today use a design with wooden frames that you can lift out, one at a time, to check on the bees. These hives are made of cedar wood, which lasts for years outdoors without needing to be treated with chemicals. That's important, because bees are very sensitive to chemicals. People often ask me how many bees live in one hive, but honestly, it varies so much through the year that I won't give you a figure. And please don't ask me what they cost, because prices change all the time. You can easily check online. Joanna: What does matter is where you put your hive. Ideally, it should face south-east, so the bees get the morning sun and start work early, and it should be sheltered from strong winds, perhaps by a hedge or a fence. Joanna: Now, this is a smoker. You burn things like dry grass or cardboard inside it, and puff a little smoke at the entrance before you open the hive. When bees sense danger, the guard bees release a warning smell, and the smoke covers it up, so the colony stays calm. Beginners nearly always use far too much smoke. Just a few puffs is all you need. Some people will tell you that the smoker is the most important piece of equipment you'll own, but I don't agree. For me, that's the hive tool, this flat metal lever here, which you use to separate the frames. Joanna: There are a few other tools you'll see around the room, but we provide everything you need during the course, so please don't buy anything yet. Right, if you'd all like to put on a suit, we'll go outside. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students called Maya and Leon discussing their research for a presentation on procrastination. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26. Leon: So, Maya, shall we go over what we've found out about procrastination? Maya: Sure. What surprised me most was just how common it is. Some surveys suggest around one adult in five describes themselves as a chronic procrastinator. Leon: And it's much higher among students, apparently. So, what about the causes? I'd always assumed it was just poor time management, people not planning properly. Maya: So had I, but most of the studies we read say that isn't really the cause. People who procrastinate usually know exactly how much time they've got. Leon: Right. It's more about emotions. If a task feels unpleasant, because it's boring or it makes you anxious, you put it off so that you feel better in the short term. Maya: Yes, I think that's the central point. And linked to that is fear of failure. If you never start something, you can't fail at it. Leon: Definitely. I recognise that in myself. What about perfectionism? Some of the articles made a big deal of that. Maya: I found that quite convincing, actually. Perfectionists set such high standards that they can't bring themselves to begin. Leon: Hmm, I'm not so sure. That big review we read said the link was actually quite weak. Maya: Fair enough. And at least we can forget the idea that procrastinators are less intelligent. There's no evidence for that at all. Leon: None. OK, then there are the effects. There was that study linking procrastination with heart disease. Maya: But that was only one study, and quite a small one. I don't think we can rely on it. Leon: True. But the link with stress is really clear. Dozens of studies show that procrastinators report higher stress levels, especially as deadlines get closer. Maya: Absolutely. And the studies on students' grades were very consistent too. The ones who put off their work got lower marks on average. Leon: Yes, that's well established. What about sleep? One paper claimed that procrastinators go to bed later. Maya: Bedtime procrastination, they called it. But all the data came from people's own reports, so I'm a bit sceptical. And I wasn't convinced by the claim about lower salaries either. There are too many other factors involved. Leon: Agreed. And what did you think of the future self theory? The idea that we treat our future selves almost like strangers, so we're happy to leave them all the hard work. Maya: I liked it. And the suggestion that you can reduce procrastination by getting people to imagine themselves in the future, by writing a letter to their future self, for example, is something people could actually use. Leon: Yes, it's practical, which is more than you can say for most theories. And it won't be hard to explain in the presentation. But the brain scan evidence behind it comes from a handful of studies with very small groups. Maya: I agree. It needs a lot more research before anyone can call it proven. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30. Maya: Should we say something about how procrastination is different from laziness? People mix them up all the time. Leon: They do. Lazy people don't really want to do anything, whereas procrastinators usually do want to do the task. They just can't make themselves start. And they often feel guilty about it. Maya: Right. I don't think there's any point in saying which one is worse, though. Leon: No. So how should we begin the presentation? I thought we could ask the class to put their hands up if they've ever left an assignment until the night before it was due. Maya: Good idea. Nearly everyone will, and it'll show straight away how widespread the problem is among students. We won't use the results as data or anything. It's just a way to get everyone involved. Leon: Then we'll move on to solutions. The one with the best evidence seems to be breaking a big task into small steps. Maya: Some articles said it works because you can tick things off and get a sense of achievement. Leon: Maybe, but I think the main thing is that a huge task feels overwhelming, and a small one doesn't. Maya: Yes, I think that's the key, really. Oh, and there was that article claiming that procrastination can actually make people more creative, because their ideas have more time to develop. Leon: I really can't see how that works. When I put things off, I just panic at the end. Maya: Me neither. It makes no sense to me at all. Anyway, shall we start putting the slides together? That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a student giving a presentation about the ways in which rooftops are used in cities. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: Today I want to talk about a part of the city that most of us never really think about, and that's the roof. If you look down on any large city from a plane, much of what you see is roofs. They make up a large proportion of the total surface area of a city, and yet the vast majority of them are completely empty. Student: It hasn't always been like this. In many hot countries, flat roofs have been used as living space for thousands of years. In parts of the Middle East and North Africa, families would sleep on the roof during hot summer nights, when it was cooler than inside the house. The roof was also a place for work. People would dry fruit and vegetables there in the sun, so that they could be stored for the winter. Student: In Europe, the story was rather different. Most roofs were steeply sloped to throw off rain and snow, so they were never meant to be used. And in the nineteenth century, as industrial cities grew, roofs became somewhere to avoid. Thousands of factory chimneys and household fires filled the air with smoke, and roofs in cities like London and Manchester were covered in a thick layer of black soot. Nobody would have wanted to spend time up there. Student: Over the last few decades, though, attitudes have changed. The first big development has been green roofs, which are roofs covered with a layer of soil and plants. Modern green roofs were developed in Germany, and they're now common in many European cities. Their great advantage is that they help to prevent flooding. When heavy rain falls on an ordinary roof, it runs straight into the drains, which can quickly overflow. A green roof, on the other hand, absorbs much of the rainwater and releases it slowly. The plants also protect the building from extreme temperatures, keeping it cooler in summer and warmer in winter, which means that the people inside have lower energy bills. Student: Some cities have gone further and started growing food on their roofs. In New York, for example, there are now several large commercial farms on top of old industrial buildings. They grow salad leaves, herbs and tomatoes. A few of them run small weekend markets, but most of their produce is sold to restaurants in the surrounding neighbourhood, which like being able to say that their ingredients were grown just a few streets away. Student: Roofs have also become important for wildlife. In Paris, beekeepers have kept hives on the roof of the famous opera house for decades, and the honey is sold to visitors. Surprisingly, city bees often do better than bees in the countryside, because parks and gardens offer a wide variety of flowers. Student: Another trend is to open roofs up to the public. In the Dutch city of Rotterdam, there's now a festival every summer when dozens of rooftops that are normally closed are opened up, with concerts, talks and guided walks high above the streets. Student: So, what about the future? One obvious use for roofs is energy production. At the moment, only a small proportion of city roofs have solar panels, but studies suggest that, in many cities, rooftop panels could generate a large share of the electricity that the buildings below them need. Student: Then there's the question of space. In crowded cities like Hong Kong, land is so expensive that some schools have built playgrounds on their roofs, surrounded by high fences, so that the children have somewhere to run around. I think we'll see much more of this in future, perhaps with rooftop sports pitches and running tracks as well. Student: Of course, there are obstacles. Some people worry about the cost, and that's certainly an issue. But the biggest problem is that most older buildings were never designed to carry anything heavy on top. Soil, water, plants and people are all surprisingly heavy, so before a roof can be used, engineers have to calculate the weight it can safely support. In many cases, the roof needs to be strengthened first. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

A full-day ticket is fifteen pounds, but if you go after one o'clock, it's twelve pounds each, and you still see the afternoon display. Tom: So twelve pounds for the afternoon. That's not bad. What about food? Kate: There's a small café. I haven't eaten there myself, but I've heard it's fairly basic. Sandwiches and crisps, that sort of thing. Tom: Well, that's fine. Thanks, Kate, that's really helpful. I think my parents will like all three. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a beekeeper called Joanna Reid talking to a group of people at the start of a beekeeping course. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Joanna: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Hillside Apiary. My name's Joanna Reid, and I've been keeping bees here for about fifteen years. This morning I'm going to give you a bit of background, then we'll go into the equipment room, and after lunch, if the weather stays fine, we'll open up one of the hives together. Joanna: People have been collecting honey for an extraordinarily long time. There are rock paintings in Spain, thousands of years old, that show someone climbing up to a wild bees' nest to take honey. But what I find really interesting is that keeping bees isn't like keeping other animals. You don't need fields or a barn. In fact, some of the most productive hives I know are on the roofs of office blocks in the city. A few square metres is really all you need. And of course, you can't tame bees or train them. They simply carry on doing what bees have always done. Joanna: So why do people take up beekeeping? When I ask people on these courses, many of them say they'd like their own honey, of course. But recently, more and more people tell me they're worried about what's happening to bees in general. You'll have read about bee numbers falling because of pesticides and disease, and people feel that by keeping a hive, they're doing something to protect them. I think that's a lovely reason, although I always point out that wild bees need help too, and planting the right flowers in your garden is just as useful. Joanna: For me personally, the best thing about beekeeping is the way it makes me pay attention to the natural world. I notice when the lime trees are flowering, or when there's been a dry spell, because the bees tell me. It's completely changed the way I see the countryside. The honey's nice, but it isn't why I do it, and it's certainly not a way to make money. Joanna: Now, most of you have never been near a hive before, and some of you might be a bit nervous about being stung. That's completely normal. Bees are generally calm if you move slowly and gently, and in all my years, I've only been stung a handful of times, usually when I was in a hurry. Actually, the people who have the most trouble aren't the nervous ones at all. It's the confident ones who rush and make sudden movements. Joanna: One practical point before we go on. Please don't wear any perfume or aftershave this afternoon. Bees find strong smells confusing, and it can make them defensive. We'll give you a protective suit, gloves and a veil, so you don't need to bring anything special, but do wear long trousers and closed shoes. Joanna: And finally, by the end of the course, some of you will want to get your own bees straight away. We can't sell you any bees ourselves, I'm afraid, but everyone who completes the course can join the local beekeepers' association for a year at half the usual price, and they'll put you in touch with an experienced mentor. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Joanna: Right, so this is our equipment room. The first thing you'll notice are the hives. Most beekeepers today use a design with wooden frames that you can lift out, one at a time, to check on the bees. These hives are made of cedar wood, which lasts for years outdoors without needing to be treated with chemicals. That's important, because bees are very sensitive to chemicals. People often ask me how many bees live in one hive, but honestly, it varies so much through the year that I won't give you a figure. And please don't ask me what they cost, because prices change all the time. You can easily check online. Joanna: What does matter is where you put your hive. Ideally, it should face south-east, so the bees get the morning sun and start work early, and it should be sheltered from strong winds, perhaps by a hedge or a fence. Joanna: Now, this is a smoker. You burn things like dry grass or cardboard inside it, and puff a little smoke at the entrance before you open the hive. When bees sense danger, the guard bees release a warning smell, and the smoke covers it up, so the colony stays calm. Beginners nearly always use far too much smoke. Just a few puffs is all you need. Some people will tell you that the smoker is the most important piece of equipment you'll own, but I don't agree. For me, that's the hive tool, this flat metal lever here, which you use to separate the frames. Joanna: There are a few other tools you'll see around the room, but we provide everything you need during the course, so please don't buy anything yet. Right, if you'd all like to put on a suit, we'll go outside. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students called Maya and Leon discussing their research for a presentation on procrastination. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26. Leon: So, Maya, shall we go over what we've found out about procrastination? Maya: Sure. What surprised me most was just how common it is. Some surveys suggest around one adult in five describes themselves as a chronic procrastinator. Leon: And it's much higher among students, apparently. So, what about the causes? I'd always assumed it was just poor time management, people not planning properly. Maya: So had I, but most of the studies we read say that isn't really the cause. People who procrastinate usually know exactly how much time they've got. Leon: Right. It's more about emotions. If a task feels unpleasant, because it's boring or it makes you anxious, you put it off so that you feel better in the short term. Maya: Yes, I think that's the central point. And linked to that is fear of failure. If you never start something, you can't fail at it. Leon: Definitely. I recognise that in myself. What about perfectionism? Some of the articles made a big deal of that. Maya: I found that quite convincing, actually. Perfectionists set such high standards that they can't bring themselves to begin. Leon: Hmm, I'm not so sure. That big review we read said the link was actually quite weak. Maya: Fair enough. And at least we can forget the idea that procrastinators are less intelligent. There's no evidence for that at all. Leon: None. OK, then there are the effects. There was that study linking procrastination with heart disease. Maya: But that was only one study, and quite a small one. I don't think we can rely on it. Leon: True. But the link with stress is really clear. Dozens of studies show that procrastinators report higher stress levels, especially as deadlines get closer. Maya: Absolutely. And the studies on students' grades were very consistent too. The ones who put off their work got lower marks on average. Leon: Yes, that's well established. What about sleep? One paper claimed that procrastinators go to bed later. Maya: Bedtime procrastination, they called it. But all the data came from people's own reports, so I'm a bit sceptical. And I wasn't convinced by the claim about lower salaries either. There are too many other factors involved. Leon: Agreed. And what did you think of the future self theory? The idea that we treat our future selves almost like strangers, so we're happy to leave them all the hard work. Maya: I liked it. And the suggestion that you can reduce procrastination by getting people to imagine themselves in the future, by writing a letter to their future self, for example, is something people could actually use. Leon: Yes, it's practical, which is more than you can say for most theories. And it won't be hard to explain in the presentation. But the brain scan evidence behind it comes from a handful of studies with very small groups. Maya: I agree. It needs a lot more research before anyone can call it proven. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30. Maya: Should we say something about how procrastination is different from laziness? People mix them up all the time. Leon: They do. Lazy people don't really want to do anything, whereas procrastinators usually do want to do the task. They just can't make themselves start. And they often feel guilty about it. Maya: Right. I don't think there's any point in saying which one is worse, though. Leon: No. So how should we begin the presentation? I thought we could ask the class to put their hands up if they've ever left an assignment until the night before it was due. Maya: Good idea. Nearly everyone will, and it'll show straight away how widespread the problem is among students. We won't use the results as data or anything. It's just a way to get everyone involved. Leon: Then we'll move on to solutions. The one with the best evidence seems to be breaking a big task into small steps. Maya: Some articles said it works because you can tick things off and get a sense of achievement. Leon: Maybe, but I think the main thing is that a huge task feels overwhelming, and a small one doesn't. Maya: Yes, I think that's the key, really. Oh, and there was that article claiming that procrastination can actually make people more creative, because their ideas have more time to develop. Leon: I really can't see how that works. When I put things off, I just panic at the end. Maya: Me neither. It makes no sense to me at all. Anyway, shall we start putting the slides together? That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a student giving a presentation about the ways in which rooftops are used in cities. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: Today I want to talk about a part of the city that most of us never really think about, and that's the roof. If you look down on any large city from a plane, much of what you see is roofs. They make up a large proportion of the total surface area of a city, and yet the vast majority of them are completely empty. Student: It hasn't always been like this. In many hot countries, flat roofs have been used as living space for thousands of years. In parts of the Middle East and North Africa, families would sleep on the roof during hot summer nights, when it was cooler than inside the house. The roof was also a place for work. People would dry fruit and vegetables there in the sun, so that they could be stored for the winter. Student: In Europe, the story was rather different. Most roofs were steeply sloped to throw off rain and snow, so they were never meant to be used. And in the nineteenth century, as industrial cities grew, roofs became somewhere to avoid. Thousands of factory chimneys and household fires filled the air with smoke, and roofs in cities like London and Manchester were covered in a thick layer of black soot. Nobody would have wanted to spend time up there. Student: Over the last few decades, though, attitudes have changed. The first big development has been green roofs, which are roofs covered with a layer of soil and plants. Modern green roofs were developed in Germany, and they're now common in many European cities. Their great advantage is that they help to prevent flooding. When heavy rain falls on an ordinary roof, it runs straight into the drains, which can quickly overflow. A green roof, on the other hand, absorbs much of the rainwater and releases it slowly. The plants also protect the building from extreme temperatures, keeping it cooler in summer and warmer in winter, which means that the people inside have lower energy bills. Student: Some cities have gone further and started growing food on their roofs. In New York, for example, there are now several large commercial farms on top of old industrial buildings. They grow salad leaves, herbs and tomatoes. A few of them run small weekend markets, but most of their produce is sold to restaurants in the surrounding neighbourhood, which like being able to say that their ingredients were grown just a few streets away. Student: Roofs have also become important for wildlife. In Paris, beekeepers have kept hives on the roof of the famous opera house for decades, and the honey is sold to visitors. Surprisingly, city bees often do better than bees in the countryside, because parks and gardens offer a wide variety of flowers. Student: Another trend is to open roofs up to the public. In the Dutch city of Rotterdam, there's now a festival every summer when dozens of rooftops that are normally closed are opened up, with concerts, talks and guided walks high above the streets. Student: So, what about the future? One obvious use for roofs is energy production. At the moment, only a small proportion of city roofs have solar panels, but studies suggest that, in many cities, rooftop panels could generate a large share of the electricity that the buildings below them need. Student: Then there's the question of space. In crowded cities like Hong Kong, land is so expensive that some schools have built playgrounds on their roofs, surrounded by high fences, so that the children have somewhere to run around. I think we'll see much more of this in future, perhaps with rooftop sports pitches and running tracks as well. Student: Of course, there are obstacles. Some people worry about the cost, and that's certainly an issue. But the biggest problem is that most older buildings were never designed to carry anything heavy on top. Soil, water, plants and people are all surprisingly heavy, so before a roof can be used, engineers have to calculate the weight it can safely support. In many cases, the roof needs to be strengthened first. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
